label: Symplectic Structures
notes: This appendix lifts symplectic geometry off the cotangent bundle. We meet manifolds that are symplectic for intrinsic reasons: coadjoint orbits, complex projective space, and homogeneous spaces. The plan is to fix the definition, flatten it with Darboux, then watch rigid bodies and fluids reappear as flows on orbits.

label: Symplectic Manifold
notes: A symplectic manifold carries a closed, nondegenerate two-form. Closedness gives a conserved structure under the flow; nondegeneracy lets every Hamiltonian function name a unique vector field. Stress that nondegeneracy forces even dimension, and that the form, not a metric, governs the dynamics here.

label: Hamiltonian Flow
notes: The form converts a differential of energy into a velocity field. Walk through the musical isomorphism: contract omega with the Hamiltonian vector field, recover dH. Because omega is closed, the flow preserves it, and Liouville volume follows as the top wedge power. This is the engine every later example rides on.

label: Darboux's Theorem
notes: Darboux says symplectic manifolds have no local invariants beyond dimension. Any point has a chart where omega becomes the constant sum dp wedge dq. Contrast sharply with Riemannian geometry, where curvature obstructs local flattening. Emphasize that all symplectic interest is therefore global, not local.

label: Linear Symplectic Geometry
notes: On a vector space the standard form pairs conjugate planes. The symplectic group consists of linear maps preserving it; its Lie algebra is the Hamiltonian matrices. Mention that the group is noncompact and connected, and that eigenvalues come in reciprocal quadruples, which controls linear stability.

label: Beyond Cotangent Bundles
notes: Not every symplectic manifold is a phase space of positions and momenta. Compact examples like spheres and projective spaces carry symplectic forms yet admit no global Darboux coordinates covering them. This motivates hunting for symplectic structures on algebraic and homogeneous manifolds directly.

label: Kahler Manifolds
notes: A Kahler manifold marries a complex structure, a metric, and a symplectic form into one compatible triple. Complex projective space is the model: the Fubini-Study form is closed and nondegenerate. Point out that the two-sphere is CP one, our first compact symplectic manifold, with area as its form.

label: Coadjoint Orbits
notes: Here is the central construction. The dual of a Lie algebra is foliated by coadjoint orbits, and each orbit carries a canonical symplectic form, the Kirillov-Kostant-Souriau form. Built purely from the Lie bracket, it needs no extra data. Every orbit is automatically even dimensional.

label: KKS Form
notes: Write the form by evaluating the point on the bracket of the two generators. Stress that the kernel of this pairing is exactly the stabilizer, so the form descends to a nondegenerate object on the orbit. This is why orbits, not the whole dual space, are the symplectic leaves.

label: Rigid Body and Fluids
notes: For SO(3) the orbits are angular-momentum spheres, and Euler's equations are Hamiltonian flow on them with the KKS area form. The same picture, on the diffeomorphism group, makes ideal fluid motion a geodesic and vorticity an orbit invariant. One construction unifies tops and turbulence.

label: Momentum Maps and Reduction
notes: A symmetry acting by symplectomorphisms produces a momentum map valued in the dual algebra; its level sets are conserved. Marsden-Weinstein reduction quotients a level set by the residual symmetry to a smaller symplectic manifold. Note that the coadjoint orbit is itself the reduction of a point.

label: Recap
notes: Recap the throughline: closed nondegenerate forms, locally trivial by Darboux, globally rich. Coadjoint orbits supply symplectic manifolds with no cotangent parentage, Kahler geometry supplies compact ones, and momentum maps tie symmetry to conserved quantities and reduction. Send students to compute the sphere's area form as the SO(3) example.
